sentences.text: For two episodes, the dial and the sliders have simply known where to stop.
Four sliders settled, the dial settled, and we read off the answers.
But nobody handed them those answers. All they had was the data: 103 patients, and who came back.
So what makes one setting of the dial and sliders better than another?
And how do they find the best one?
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: fitting by balance.
Start with any setting at all. Here is the plainest: every patient, at every clinic, gets the overall rate, 41%.
Now ask of each patient: what probability did this guess give to what actually happened?
For a patient who was readmitted, 41%. For one who wasn't, 59%.
Multiply those 103 numbers together, and you have the probability the guess gave to the whole story. That is its likelihood.
It is tiny: a decimal point followed by thirty zeros. So we take its logarithm instead: minus 69.6.
Think of that number as a height. A better guess stands higher.
The height itself means nothing. Only the climb from one guess to another does.
So which way is up? Bring back the meter from Episode 3: observed on one side, expected on the other.
Here is one for every clinic, under the plain guess.
Dune expected 4.9 readmissions and saw 7. Birch expected 12.2 and saw 14. Elm expected 4.5 and saw none.
And here is the fact that makes fitting possible.
Each meter's tilt is exactly the slope of the height in that clinic's gamma.
Observed above expected: push the slider up. Observed below: pull it down.
Try it with Dune. Push its slider up, and among the clinics, only Dune's meter responds.
Its expected count climbs toward 7, and the height rises with it.
When the meter is level, the height is as high as this one slider can take it.
Push further, and the meter tips the other way. The height falls.
The dial has a meter too. It weighs only the higher-risk patients: 29 of them were readmitted, and the plain guess expected fewer than 19.
Turn the dial up until that meter is level.
But look at the clinics. Every one that has higher-risk patients has shifted.
So nothing can be settled one piece at a time. The dial and the sliders have to find their places together.
And here is where they stop. The dial at 2.02, and the sliders where we found them two episodes ago.
Four clinic meters are level, and so is the dial's.
In each of those four clinics, expected now equals observed: 13, 14, 8 and 7.
That is what fitting is: balancing.
One detail. The balance holds for each clinic's total, not for each group inside it.
Alder expected 8.2 among its lower-risk patients and 4.8 among its higher-risk ones. Not 8 and 5. But together, 13.
And Elm? Its meter can never level. With no readmissions, expected stays above observed wherever the slider sits.
So the slider keeps sliding, gaining a little less height each time. We'll come back to Elm.
With Elm's slider run all the way down, the height has climbed from minus 69.6 to minus 55.6.
One last picture. For each position of the dial, level the clinics' meters, and record the height.
The result is a hill, with one top, at 2.02.
The pooled step from Episode 3, 1.75, sits a little way down the left side.
And notice how gently the top is rounded. That gentleness is the roughness we keep promising to measure.
Let's gather it up.
A guess is scored by the probability it gave to what actually happened.
Each clinic's meter, observed minus expected, says which way its slider should move.
And at the best fit, every meter that can level is level.
A caution. Level meters do not show that the model is right.
Any model with a number for each clinic will level them. Whether it is right has to be judged inside the clinics, and that comes later.
We have seen where the top of the hill is, not how to get there. No formula gives it.
Next time: climbing the hill.
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
